blocks.body:
If $r$ and $s$ are the roots of $x^2 - 7x + 10$, then without solving anything you can say $r + s = 7$ and $rs = 10$ (the roots are $2$ and $5$). This link between the roots of a polynomial and its coefficients, together with a handful of facts about division of polynomials, solves a surprising share of algebra problems: finding remainders, counting roots, reconstructing a polynomial from a few of its values.

This page covers the factor theorem, the bound on the number of roots, Vieta's formulas for any degree, and Lagrange interpolation. Coefficients are real or complex numbers throughout; the last pitfall explains what changes for other number systems.

blocks.title: Polynomial, degree, root
blocks.body:
A polynomial is an expression $P(x) = a_nx^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_1x + a_0$ with coefficients $a_i$. If $a_n \ne 0$, the degree is $n$ and $a_n$ is the leading coefficient; $P$ is monic if $a_n = 1$. The zero polynomial has no degree. A root (or zero) of $P$ is a number $a$ with $P(a) = 0$.

Two polynomials are equal when their coefficients agree; one of the results below shows this is the same as having equal values at enough points.

blocks.title: Division with remainder
blocks.body:
Polynomials can be divided like integers. For polynomials $P$ and $D$ with $D \ne 0$ there are unique polynomials $Q$ (quotient) and $R$ (remainder) with

$$P = DQ + R,\qquad R = 0 \text{ or } \deg R < \deg D.$$

They are found by long division: repeatedly subtract a multiple of $D$ that cancels the current leading term. (We omit the formal proof, which is an induction on $\deg P$.)

The most important case is division by $x - a$, where the remainder is a constant. Substituting $x = a$ into $P(x) = (x - a)Q(x) + R$ shows that $R = P(a)$: the remainder on dividing by $x - a$ is the value at $a$. For example $x^3 - 2x + 5$ leaves remainder $8 - 4 + 5 = 9$ on division by $x - 2$.

blocks.title: Factor theorem
blocks.body:
For a polynomial $P$ and a number $a$,

$$P(a) = 0 \iff (x-a) \mid P(x).$$
Divide: $P(x) = (x - a)Q(x) + P(a)$. If $P(a) = 0$ this exhibits $x - a$ as a factor. Conversely, if $P(x) = (x - a)Q(x)$, then $P(a) = 0\cdot Q(a) = 0$.

blocks.title: A polynomial of degree n has at most n roots
blocks.body: A nonzero polynomial of degree $n$ with real or complex coefficients has at most $n$ distinct roots. Consequently, if two polynomials of degree at most $n$ take equal values at $n + 1$ distinct points, they are equal (identical coefficients).

Induction on $n$. A nonzero constant ($n = 0$) has no roots. Let $\deg P = n \ge 1$. If $P$ has no root we are done. Otherwise let $a$ be a root; by the factor theorem $P(x) = (x - a)Q(x)$ with $\deg Q = n - 1$. If $b \ne a$ is another root then $0 = P(b) = (b - a)Q(b)$, and since $b - a \ne 0$, we get $Q(b) = 0$. So every root of $P$ other than $a$ is a root of $Q$, which has at most $n - 1$ roots by induction. In total $P$ has at most $n$ roots.

For the consequence, if $P$ and $\tilde P$ have degree at most $n$ and agree at $n + 1$ points, then $P - \tilde P$ has degree at most $n$ (or is zero) and has $n + 1$ roots, so it must be the zero polynomial.

blocks.title: Factoring completely
blocks.body:
Over the complex numbers every nonconstant polynomial has a root: this is the fundamental theorem of algebra (proof omitted; see [[complex-numbers]]). Applying the factor theorem repeatedly, a polynomial of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $a_n$ factors completely as

$$P(x) = a_n(x - r_1)(x - r_2)\cdots(x - r_n),$$

where $r_1, \dots, r_n$ are its complex roots listed with multiplicity (a root appearing $k$ times in the list is a root of multiplicity $k$). So "at most $n$ roots" becomes "exactly $n$ roots counted with multiplicity" over $\mathbb C$.

blocks.title: Elementary symmetric polynomials
blocks.body:
For numbers $r_1, \dots, r_n$ and $1 \le k \le n$, the $k$-th elementary symmetric polynomial $e_k$ is the sum of all products of $k$ of the numbers with distinct indices:

$$e_1 = \sum_i r_i,\qquad e_2 = \sum_{i<j}r_ir_j,\qquad \dots,\qquad e_n = r_1r_2\cdots r_n.$$

So $e_k$ has $\binom nk$ terms. For three numbers: $e_1 = r+s+t$, $e_2 = rs+st+tr$, $e_3 = rst$.

blocks.title: Vieta's formulas
blocks.body:
For any numbers $r_1, \dots, r_n$,

$$\prod_{i=1}^n (x - r_i) = x^n - e_1x^{n-1} + e_2x^{n-2} - \cdots + (-1)^n e_n.$$

Hence, if $P(x) = a_nx^n + \cdots + a_0$ has roots $r_1, \dots, r_n$ (with multiplicity), then $e_k = (-1)^k\,a_{n-k}/a_n$ for $k = 1, \dots, n$. For a quadratic $ax^2 + bx + c$: $r + s = -b/a$ and $rs = c/a$.

Expand the product $(x - r_1)(x - r_2)\cdots(x - r_n)$ by choosing, from each factor, either $x$ or $-r_i$, and adding up all $2^n$ choices. A choice that takes $-r_i$ from exactly the factors indexed by a set $S$ of size $k$ and $x$ from the others contributes $(-1)^k\big(\prod_{i\in S}r_i\big)x^{n-k}$. Summing over all sets $S$ of size $k$ gives the coefficient $(-1)^ke_k$ of $x^{n-k}$.

For a general $P$, write $P(x) = a_n\prod(x - r_i)$ and compare coefficients of $x^{n-k}$: $a_{n-k} = a_n(-1)^ke_k$.

blocks.title: Lagrange interpolation
blocks.body:
Given $n + 1$ points $(x_0, y_0), \dots, (x_n, y_n)$ with distinct $x_i$, there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most $n$ passing through them:

$$P(x) = \sum_{i=0}^n y_i\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{x - x_j}{x_i - x_j}.$$

The $i$-th product equals $1$ at $x_i$ and $0$ at every other $x_j$, so $P(x_i) = y_i$; uniqueness is the "agree at $n + 1$ points" consequence above.

Example: through $(1, 2)$, $(2, 3)$, $(3, 6)$,

$$P(x) = 2\cdot\frac{(x-2)(x-3)}{(1-2)(1-3)} + 3\cdot\frac{(x-1)(x-3)}{(2-1)(2-3)} + 6\cdot\frac{(x-1)(x-2)}{(3-1)(3-2)} = x^2 - 2x + 3.$$

In competitions interpolation is used less to compute $P$ than to prove things about it: knowing a polynomial at enough points determines it, so one constructs a candidate that obviously has the right values.
Let $r, s, t$ be the complex roots of $x^3 - 2x^2 + 3x - 4$. Compute $r^2 + s^2 + t^2$ and $\tfrac1r + \tfrac1s + \tfrac1t$. What does the first answer say about the roots?
blocks.solution:
By Vieta, $e_1 = 2$, $e_2 = 3$, $e_3 = 4$ (signs: $x^3 - e_1x^2 + e_2x - e_3$).

Since $(r+s+t)^2 = r^2+s^2+t^2 + 2(rs+st+tr)$,

$$r^2 + s^2 + t^2 = e_1^2 - 2e_2 = 4 - 6 = -2.$$

Also $\tfrac1r + \tfrac1s + \tfrac1t = \tfrac{st + tr + rs}{rst} = \tfrac{e_2}{e_3} = \tfrac34$.

A sum of squares of real numbers cannot be negative, so the roots are not all real. (A real cubic always has at least one real root, so exactly one root is real and the other two are complex conjugates.)
blocks.title: Symmetric functions of roots without finding them

blocks.body: Find the remainder when $x^{100}$ is divided by $x^2 - 3x + 2$.
blocks.solution:
The divisor has degree $2$, so $x^{100} = (x^2 - 3x + 2)Q(x) + ax + b$ for some constants $a, b$. Since $x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x-1)(x-2)$ vanishes at $x = 1$ and $x = 2$, substituting these values gives

$$1 = a + b,\qquad 2^{100} = 2a + b.$$

Subtracting, $a = 2^{100} - 1$, and then $b = 1 - a = 2 - 2^{100}$. The remainder is

$$(2^{100} - 1)x + 2 - 2^{100}.$$
blocks.title: A remainder without long division

blocks.body: A monic polynomial $P$ of degree $4$ satisfies $P(1) = 1$, $P(2) = 2$, $P(3) = 3$, $P(4) = 4$. Find $P(5)$ and $P(0)$.
blocks.solution:
The values say $P(k) - k = 0$ for $k = 1, 2, 3, 4$. So $Q(x) = P(x) - x$ is a monic polynomial of degree $4$ with roots $1, 2, 3, 4$. By the factor theorem and comparison of degrees and leading coefficients,

$$Q(x) = (x-1)(x-2)(x-3)(x-4).$$

Hence $P(5) = 4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1 + 5 = 29$ and $P(0) = (-1)(-2)(-3)(-4) + 0 = 24$.

The lesson: when a polynomial takes "nice" values at several points, subtract the obvious function with those values and look at the roots of the difference.
blocks.title: Use the factor theorem on a cleverly chosen polynomial

blocks.body: A polynomial $P$ of degree at most $n$ satisfies $P(k) = 2^k$ for $k = 0, 1, \dots, n$. Find $P(n+1)$.
blocks.solution:
The trick from the previous example does not apply directly ($2^x$ is not a polynomial), so build the candidate by hand. For each $j$, the binomial coefficient

$$\binom xj = \frac{x(x-1)\cdots(x-j+1)}{j!}$$

is a polynomial in $x$ of degree $j$. Let $Q(x) = \sum_{j=0}^n\binom xj$, a polynomial of degree $n$. For an integer $k$ with $0 \le k \le n$ we have $\binom kj = 0$ when $j > k$, so

$$Q(k) = \sum_{j=0}^k\binom kj = 2^k$$

by the binomial theorem ([[binomial-factorial]]). Thus $P$ and $Q$ have degree at most $n$ and agree at the $n + 1$ points $0, 1, \dots, n$, so $P = Q$. Finally

$$P(n+1) = \sum_{j=0}^n\binom{n+1}{j} = 2^{n+1} - \binom{n+1}{n+1} = 2^{n+1} - 1.$$

For instance with $n = 2$: $P(x) = 1 + x + \tfrac{x(x-1)}{2}$ has values $1, 2, 4$ at $0, 1, 2$ and $P(3) = 7$.
blocks.title: Interpolation with binomial coefficients

blocks.body:
- Roots are counted with multiplicity in Vieta's formulas: $(x-1)^2(x+2) = x^3 - 3x + 2$ has roots $1, 1, -2$, and $e_1 = 0$, $e_2 = -3$, $e_3 = -2$ only if $1$ is listed twice.
- Vieta uses all $n$ roots, complex ones included. Applying it to "the real roots" of a cubic with only one real root gives nonsense.
- Watch the alternating signs: the coefficient of $x^{n-1}$ is $-e_1$, not $e_1$.
- Comparing coefficients is valid for an identity that holds for all $x$ (or at least at more points than the degree), not for an equation that holds at a few points.
- "At most $n$ roots" uses the fact that a product of two nonzero numbers is nonzero. In arithmetic modulo $8$ this fails ($2\cdot 4 \equiv 0$), and indeed $x^2 - 1$ has four roots modulo $8$: $1, 3, 5, 7$. The theorem holds for coefficients in any field, such as $\mathbb Z/p$ for a prime $p$ ([[finite-fields]]).

Vieta's formulas are the engine of [[vieta-jumping]], where one root of a quadratic is traded for the other, and of the $p, q, r$ method in [[symmetric-ineq]]. For a matrix, the characteristic polynomial has the eigenvalues as roots, so by Vieta the sum of the [[eigen|eigenvalues]] is the trace and their product is the determinant. Adjoining roots of polynomials to a field is the starting point of [[fields-ext|field extensions]] and of [[galois]] theory, and polynomials with integer coefficients have their own arithmetic ([[integer-polynomials]]).

Sets of common zeros of polynomials in several variables are the objects of algebraic geometry; one of its deepest open problems, the [[hodge]] conjecture, asks whether certain topological features (rational Hodge classes) of smooth complex projective varieties always come from algebraic subvarieties, as rational combinations of their classes. In combinatorics, the fact that a nonzero polynomial cannot vanish too often is the basis of the polynomial method.

1. If $r$ and $s$ are the roots of $x^2 - 5x + 3$, find $r^3 + s^3$ without solving the equation.
2. Find the remainder when $x^{2026}$ is divided by $x^2 - 1$.
3. Prove that a real polynomial with $P(x) = P(x + 1)$ for all real $x$ is constant.
4. Find the polynomial of degree at most $2$ through $(0, 1)$, $(1, 3)$ and $(2, 7)$.
